hook: A factory making ammonia needs to know how much product it will get from a tank of nitrogen and hydrogen before it builds the reactor. Nobody can wait for the gases to settle and measure. Instead, engineers take the equilibrium constant, the starting amounts and a three-row table, and calculate exactly what the mixture will hold at equilibrium.

prereq.q: In an ICE table for A ⇌ 2 B, if A changes by −x, what is the change in B?
prereq.why: Changes follow the coefficients: 1 A used makes 2 B.

prereq.q: A mixture has Q > K. Which way does the net reaction go?
options: It depends on the temperature only
prereq.why: Q > K means too much product, so the reaction runs in reverse until Q = K.

prereq.q: For a reaction with K = 1 × 10<sup>−8</sup>, starting from reactants, how much reactant is left at equilibrium?
prereq.why: A tiny K means a reactant-favored equilibrium: very little reacts.

figure.caption: Direction, ICE table, substitute, then solve by square root, small-x approximation or the quadratic formula, and check.

chain.cause: Q is compared with K for the starting mixture
chain.effect: you know which side is used up and which forms

chain.cause: The ICE table writes each change as ±x times a coefficient
chain.effect: every equilibrium concentration is written with one unknown

chain.cause: The Equilibrium row is substituted into the K expression
chain.effect: you get one equation in x

chain.cause: K is small compared with the starting concentration
chain.effect: x can be dropped from (initial − x), and a 5% check confirms it
every equilibrium concentration follows from Initial + Change

ideas: Always find the direction first by comparing Q with K; it sets the signs in the Change row.
Changes are ±x × coefficient. Equilibrium = Initial + Change. Use molarities.
Perfect square: take the square root of both sides. Small K: drop x only from (initial − x), never x standing alone.
Check the small-x approximation: the change must be under about 5% of the starting value; otherwise solve exactly.

misconception.wrong: If K is small, x is small, so every x in the equation can be set to zero.
misconception.right: Only x that is added to or subtracted from a larger number can be dropped: 0.50 − 2x ≈ 0.50. The x terms standing alone on top of the expression stay, or there is nothing left to solve. Then check the 5% rule.

summary: To find equilibrium concentrations from K, compare Q with K to get the direction, build an ICE table with changes of ±x times each coefficient, substitute the Equilibrium row into K and solve for x. A perfect-square expression is solved by a square root. When K is small compared with the starting concentration, x can be dropped from (initial − x) but never set to zero elsewhere, and the result must pass the 5% check; otherwise use the quadratic formula.
